record.tranche_reason: The study measures feature geometry and tests feature directions in a trained gridworld transformer using cosine similarity, PCA, embedding edits, and direct interventions. This is a conceptual test of superposition-related claims, not a reproduction of the original toy-model method.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own embedding-geometry analyses and feature interventions. Results cited from toy-model and language-model studies are not recorded. Several plotted results are described qualitatively in the text, but their individual plotted values are not provided.
record.test_reason: The study analyses learned observation embeddings in a trained gridworld decision transformer (MemoryDT) and reports superposition-style geometry: antipodal pairs for anti-correlated items, plus isotropic and anisotropic clusters. It also reports a causally validated linear feature direction. This is a new setting with its own results on V1, and weakly on V6, rather than a reproduction of the toy-model sparsity sweep, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MemoryDT's embeddings have extensive geometric structure, including clusters, antipodal pairs, and isotropic (target) and anisotropic (instruction) superposition. They identify linear features 'smeared' across embeddings and causally validate the instruction feature, saying the adversaries act entirely through it. They caution against generalising from one model to language models.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes a trained gridworld decision transformer’s observation embeddings with cosine similarity, PCA, and causal feature interventions; it does not use the original toy-model setup or sweep feature sparsity.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports different geometry for instruction and target embedding subsets; instruction-direction effects also vary across target/instruction configurations and RTG settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Feature-level adversarial inputs (decoy complement objects) partially flip the model's action preference: restored logit difference mostly 0.80-0.90 with two decoys. The same adversaries transfer to MemoryDT-GatedMLP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Antipodal or anisotropic superposed features can be exploited by targeted adversarial inputs, and such adversaries transfer across similar models.

record.problems: Evidence comes from one gridworld model and selected embedding subsets. The study does not vary sparsity or compare feature count with dimensions. Several findings are described from figures without individual numerical values, and the authors note ambiguity in interpreting PC2 and that the model does not consistently implement the task’s XOR rule.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were omitted. Individual plotted values not stated in the text were not reconstructed.

untested.parts: There is no sparsity or importance sweep, no phase transition, and no explicit count of features versus dimensions (vocabulary of 7x7x20 items against 256 dims is never analysed as such). Only selected embedding subsets are examined.
There is no test of whether any features are multi-dimensional. The author only raises the possibility of subspaces or manifolds in a comment.
Not tested: there is no neuron-level polysemanticity analysis.
Not tested: the model is not an LLM and no SAE is used.

missing.what: Transfer of the instruction adversaries to MemoryDT-GatedMLP, where reversal was closer to or exceeded the positive control.
missing.locator: Results, 'Do the Instruction Feature Adversaries Transfer?'; Figure 20

missing.what: L2 norm distribution: task-important key/ball channels have the largest norms. This is loosely relevant to importance-weighted representation, but it is not a neuron-level result.
missing.locator: Results, 'Geometric Structure in Embedding Space'; Figure 5

record.verdict_notes: The reader's tranche is changed from T2 to T3 because this is a new setting rather than a method aimed at the toy-model question. R5 and R7 are unlinked from V6 because they measure adversary efficacy, not feature dimensionality. R3 is removed from the V1 label. Embedding superposition here concerns vocabulary-item embeddings rather than hidden-layer activations. Single post, one model, no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not vary feature sparsity or importance, measure whether the number of features exceeds the embedding dimension, or test a sparsity-dependent transition. It reports geometry in selected embedding subsets, not a general regular geometry across settings.
The study does not test neuron polysemanticity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared capacity.
The study does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
The model is a gridworld decision transformer, not an LLM; the study does not measure feature spread across LLM neurons or SAE recovery.
The study does not test whether dictionary features are complete, stable, or canonical units.

The study identifies and causally tests an instruction-feature direction, but does not compare 1-D and multidimensional feature representations generally or establish that all superposed features are 1-D.

rows.subject: MemoryDT
rows.size_stated: over a million parameters (comment); observation embedding vector length 256
rows.operation_detail: Measured cosine similarities among learned observation vocabulary-item embeddings.

conditions.value: Key/Ball channels and other vocabulary-item groups

rows.value: The study reports clusters and antipodal pairs. Keys and balls at the same positions showed negative cosine-similarity lines, consistent with spatial exclusivity; some correlated vocabulary items had high cosine similarity. The authors describe instruction-related and target-related groups with different geometric patterns.
rows.locator: Results, “Cosine Similarity Heatmaps Reveal Geometric Structure”; Figures 6–8
rows.note: The text gives qualitative descriptions; individual cosine values are not reported there.
rows.check: State is fine. The text links antipodality to spatial anti-correlation, consistent with toy-model geometry, but gives no cosine values. No baseline is stated; the low-norm, untrained embeddings act as an informal contrast.

source_check.locator_found: Cosine Similarity Heatmaps Reveal Geometric Structure, Figures 6–8; lines 161–193.

rows.subject: MemoryDT
rows.size_stated: over a million parameters (comment); observation embedding vector length 256
rows.operation_detail: Applied PCA to the selected instruction-related embedding vectors and examined component projections across key/ball embeddings.

conditions.value: Instruction embeddings at positions identified as instruction-visible

rows.measure: Explained variance and interpretation of principal components
rows.value: The first two principal components explain 85.12% of the variance. PC1 separates keys from balls independently of position; its feature map shows the direction present to varying degrees in embeddings at multiple positions. The subset also forms antipodal key/ball pairs in the first two components.
rows.note: The authors identify PC1 as a candidate instruction-feature direction and describe the geometry as resembling anisotropic superposition.
rows.check: Add that PC1 alone explains about 60% of variance across the 6 vectors (Embedding Arithmetic section). The geometry is anisotropic rather than toy-model isotropic, which matters for the V1 label. The authors also ask why the pairs 'weren't they more antipodal'.

source_check.correct: State: partial for V1; observed for V6. The instruction geometry is anisotropic and incompletely antipodal. The first two PCs explain 85.12% of variance; PC1 separates keys from balls independently of position.
source_check.locator_found: The Primary Instruction Feature, Figures 9–10, lines 201–215; discussion, lines 342–348.
source_check.problem: A single observed state obscures the incomplete match to V1 geometry, which the record itself labels limits_scope.

rows.subject: MemoryDT
rows.size_stated: over a million parameters (comment); observation embedding vector length 256
rows.operation_detail: Examined the second principal component of the instruction-embedding subset and its projections across key/ball embeddings.
rows.measure: Interpretability of the component's feature map
rows.value: PC2 distinguishes some starting versus look-back observations, but the proposed interpretation does not fit all projections; the authors say they suspect PCA did not find a second interpretable feature direction and that a meaningful underlying feature remains possible.
rows.note: This is an unresolved component, not evidence that a second feature is absent.
rows.check: An unresolved PC2 cannot show whether the instruction representation is 1-D or multi-dimensional. It should not carry a V1 label, which the reader's limits_scope label currently gives it.

rows.subject: MemoryDT
rows.size_stated: over a million parameters (comment); observation embedding vector length 256
rows.operation_detail: Applied PCA to the selected target-related embedding vectors and interpreted the resulting components.
rows.measure: Explained variance and geometric pattern of principal components
rows.value: The first two principal components explain 83.69% of the variance. The embeddings form two clusters, each with two nearly antipodal pairs. The authors interpret PC1 as a starting-target feature and PC2 as an end-target feature, and describe the geometry as closer to isotropic superposition.
rows.note: The authors also describe a faint checkerboard pattern as a possible hint of a broader target feature.
rows.check: None. The authors describe the target geometry as much closer to isotropic superposition, which matches V1.

rows.subject: MemoryDT
rows.size_stated: over a million parameters (comment); observation embedding vector length 256
rows.operation_detail: Measured the instruction-direction projection of edited first-frame observation embeddings against the left-versus-right logit difference.

conditions.value: Tested target/instruction configurations and RTG settings
Original instruction and added complement objects

rows.measure: Instruction-feature projection and left-minus-right logit difference
rows.baseline: Original frame as negative control; instruction-flipped frame as positive control
rows.value: The two-complement input did not project as strongly into the instruction direction as the instruction-flipped input. Flipping the sign of the direction often flipped action preference, but not in the Key-Ball, RTG = 0.892 case. The relation between projection and logit difference varied across scenarios.
rows.locator: Results, “The adversarial inputs are changing the presence of the instruction feature”; Figure 18
rows.note: The text describes the plotted relationships and exceptions but does not report the individual plotted values.
rows.check: This row measures how strongly the adversary moves the projection, and the model's XOR implementation (the Key-Ball, RTG 0.892 failure). Neither bears on whether superposed features are 1-D, so it should not be linked to V6.

rows.subject: MemoryDT
rows.size_stated: over a million parameters (comment); observation embedding vector length 256
rows.operation_detail: Directly intervened on the instruction PC0 direction and measured the resulting left-minus-right logit difference.

conditions.value: Same scenarios as the instruction-adversary experiment

rows.value: The direct intervention produces a mapping described as similar to, and clearer than, the mapping from the adversarial-input experiment; the authors say it suggests the instruction feature explains the adversarial results.

rows.note: The figure’s individual numerical values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: It shows that a single direction causally controls the logit difference. It does not compare this against a multi-dimensional representation. Locator should read PC0 (figure naming) / PC1 (text).

rows.subject: MemoryDT
rows.size_stated: over a million parameters (comment); observation embedding vector length 256
rows.operation_detail: Added complement vocabulary items to the first observation as predicted by the instruction-feature direction.

conditions.value: Complement at (0,5), at (4,2), or at both positions
Target/instruction configurations and RTG combinations in the experiment

rows.measure: Proportion of left/right logit difference restored relative to the negative and positive controls
rows.baseline: Original frame as negative control; instruction-flipped frame as positive control
rows.value: The best two-decoy result was 0.92, and most results were around 0.80–0.90. Single-decoy effects were inconsistent; in the Ball, Ball-Key, RTG = 0 case, one complement restored 0.43 of the two-complement logit difference and the other 0.03.

rows.note: The authors say the two decoys did not work as well as reversing the original instruction. The reported values summarize multiple scenarios rather than supplying each plotted value.
rows.check: Restored logit difference from decoy inputs measures how effective the adversary is, not feature dimensionality or superposition geometry. Unlink it from V6.
